title: My Fraction Stories
author: Josh Fisher
summary: Josh Fisher introduces the concept of 'fraction stories'—expert-facing instructional sketches that outline a complete pedagogical thought without being lesson plans—and presents his first: All Whole Numbers Are Fractions. His diagnosis of fraction difficulty is that fractions are introduced as alien newcomers rather than extensions of number families students already know, producing the well-documented 'whole-number bias.' His proposed corrective is to start fraction instruction by demonstrating that whole numbers already have denominators (3/1, 6/1) and that the rules governing fraction arithmetic are rules students have been following all along, just without the notation. The piece is addressed to math educators and researchers, and is notable for treating instructional sequencing as a hypothesis to be tested rather than a tradition to be transmitted.
points: Fisher introduces 'fraction stories'—expert-to-expert instructional sketches that outline a complete pedagogical idea without being student-facing lesson plans.
His diagnosis: fractions are introduced as foreign and strange rather than as extensions of number families students already know, which systematically produces the 'whole-number bias.'
The first story proposes beginning fraction instruction by demonstrating that all whole numbers are already fractions (3/1, 6/1), making the alien familiar before introducing genuinely new concepts.
The explicit goal is to see whether restoring continuity between whole numbers and fractions can reduce or eliminate the whole-number bias that causes persistent student difficulty.
The piece is a model of treating instructional sequencing as falsifiable hypothesis rather than inherited practice—inviting educator commentary as a necessary part of the 'story' format.
quotes: A 'story,' to me, is a kind of pedagogical back-of-the-napkin sketch—an outline of a 'complete thought,' instructionally. It is not a lesson; it is less complicated and no student will see it.
Almost no students are immune to difficulties with fractions and for many students, year after year, they remain a significant obstacle. So something in and/or around the fraction story is busted.
We should not say that fractions are 'just hard'; we should see if making the story simpler will help.

Fractions are introduced to us as foreign and alien. A new family has moved into town, the Fractions, and boy are they strange—less is more but also more is more, they're always in pairs, they have weird names, strange rules and customs.
Why not give students 3/1 + 6/1 = [ ] and let them see that those strange customs aren't strange at all—you follow them yourself?
